note: Every relationship carries a verification grade and an evidence/source pointer. Disputed and provisional items are preserved, not harmonized.

relationships.description: Chicago DJ/producer Jesse Saunders recorded and released "On and On" on his Jes Say Records label in early 1984; it is widely cited as the first house track committed to vinyl.
relationships.evidence: Resident Advisor notes "On and On" was put on vinyl in early 1984 by Saunders and engineer Vince Lawrence and is 'generally accepted as the first house track committed to vinyl'; the release drew partly on a Mach "On & On" bootleg megamix.
relationships.source: Resident Advisor (ra.co/news/10915); Wikipedia "On & On (Jesse Saunders song)"

relationships.description: Vince Lawrence co-wrote and co-produced "On and On" with Jesse Saunders and engineered the record.
relationships.evidence: RA credits Saunders and engineer Vince Lawrence with putting "On and On" on vinyl; NPR/KMUC documents Lawrence as Saunders's collaborator in the early Mitchbal/Chicago Connection recordings.

relationships.description: Saunders and Lawrence were collaborators in Chicago's earliest house productions, working together on the Mitchbal/Chicago Connection recordings and "On and On."
relationships.evidence: NPR/KMUC describes Lawrence as Saunders's friend and collaborator; RA documents their joint work on "On and On."

relationships.description: Jamie Principle's "Your Love" circulated on cassette in Chicago clubs before its April 1986 vinyl release on Persona Records — i.e., it was heard as house music before "On and On" was pressed to vinyl.
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia documents pre-vinyl club circulation on cassette and the April 1986 Persona release; RA notes the 'mythology and confusion' around firsts.
relationships.source: Wikipedia "Your Love (Jamie Principle song)"; Resident Advisor

relationships.description: The 1987 Trax Records version of "Your Love" was credited to Frankie Knuckles; Principle alleged in 2014 that Trax 'literally just stole my stuff.' Authorship/credit is contested.
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia records the 1987 Trax Knuckles-credited version and Principle's 2014 allegation; no adjudicated finding located.

relationships.description: Frankie Knuckles was resident DJ at the Warehouse from 1977 to 1982, the foundational residency of Chicago house.
relationships.evidence: City of Chicago Warehouse landmark report documents Knuckles's 1977–1982 association with the Warehouse at 206 S. Jefferson.
relationships.source: City of Chicago, 'The Warehouse' landmark designation report (chicago.gov)

relationships.description: After leaving the Warehouse in late 1982, Knuckles founded his own club, the Power Plant, at 1015 N. Halsted in 1983.
relationships.evidence: City of Chicago Warehouse report records Knuckles leaving Robert Williams's operation and founding the Power Plant in 1983.
relationships.source: City of Chicago, 'The Warehouse' landmark designation report
relationships.to: The Power Plant (1015 N. Halsted St.)

relationships.description: Ron Hardy became resident DJ of Robert Williams's Music Box when it opened in February 1983 at 1632 S. Indiana Avenue.
relationships.evidence: Red Bull Music Academy's Ron Hardy history places the original Music Box at 1632 S. Indiana Ave. in February 1983 with Hardy as resident, quoting Williams directly.
relationships.to: The Music Box (1632 S. Indiana Ave.)

relationships.description: Promoter Robert Williams opened the Warehouse, and after Knuckles's 1982 departure he hired Ron Hardy for the Music Box.
relationships.evidence: City landmark report documents Williams's role and the hiring of Hardy; RBMA quotes Williams on the Music Box's founding.
relationships.source: City of Chicago Warehouse report; Red Bull Music Academy Daily (2015-05)

relationships.description: The genre name 'house music' derives from the Warehouse club, where Knuckles's sets defined the early sound.
relationships.evidence: City landmark report ties the genre's naming to the Warehouse; the 2004 honorary street designation 'Frankie Knuckles Way' at 206 S. Jefferson recognizes this history.
relationships.source: City of Chicago, 'The Warehouse' landmark designation report

relationships.description: WBMX program director Lee Michaels selected the founding Hot Mix 5 lineup in 1981 for 'Saturday Night Live, Ain't No Jive.'
relationships.evidence: Hot Mix 5 history credits Michaels with choosing the five DJs in 1981.

relationships.description: Farley Keith was a founding member of WBMX's Hot Mix 5 in 1981.
relationships.evidence: Hot Mix 5 founding lineup lists Farley 'Funkin' Keith among the five DJs chosen by Lee Michaels.

relationships.description: Mickey Oliver was a founding member of WBMX's Hot Mix 5 in 1981.
relationships.evidence: Founding lineup as documented in Hot Mix 5 history.

relationships.description: Ralphi Rosario was a founding member of WBMX's Hot Mix 5 in 1981.
relationships.evidence: Founding lineup as documented in Hot Mix 5 history.

relationships.description: Kenny Jason was a founding member of WBMX's Hot Mix 5 in 1981.
relationships.evidence: Founding lineup as documented in Hot Mix 5 history.

relationships.description: Scott Silz was a founding member of WBMX's Hot Mix 5 in 1981.
relationships.evidence: Founding lineup as documented in Hot Mix 5 history.

relationships.description: The Hot Mix 5's live mixes reached a massive Chicago audience; the City's Warehouse report cites roughly one million weekly listeners, while other accounts claim two million.
relationships.evidence: City landmark report gives ~1M weekly; Hot Mix 5 history claims 2M and #1 ratings. Audience figure varies by source.
relationships.source: City of Chicago Warehouse report; Wikipedia "Hot Mix 5"

relationships.description: Farley Keith guest-DJ'd at the Warehouse and was later resident at the Playground, linking the Hot Mix 5 radio crew to the club scene.
relationships.evidence: Hot Mix 5 history notes Farley's Warehouse guest sets and Playground residency.

relationships.description: DJ Pierre was a founding member of Phuture alongside Spanky and Herb J.
relationships.evidence: Georgia Entertainment profiles Phuture's three members and their TB-303/TR-707 experiments.

relationships.description: Earl 'Spanky' Smith Jr. was a founding member of Phuture.
relationships.evidence: Georgia Entertainment member profile.

relationships.description: Herbert 'Herb J' Jackson was a founding member of Phuture.
relationships.evidence: Georgia Entertainment member profile.

relationships.description: Phuture's experiments with the Roland TB-303 bass synthesizer (and TR-707) generated the squelching sound that defines acid house.
relationships.evidence: Georgia Entertainment and MusicRadar document Phuture's TB-303 experiments as the origin of the acid sound.

relationships.description: Phuture created 'Acid Tracks'; Ron Hardy tested it at the Music Box before its 1987 vinyl pressing.
relationships.evidence: MusicRadar and Georgia Entertainment document the track's creation, Hardy's club testing, and 1987 pressing.

relationships.description: Hardy was given 'Acid Tracks' by Phuture and famously played it four times in one night at the Music Box, breaking the record.
relationships.evidence: MusicRadar reports Hardy playing it four times in a single night.

relationships.description: "I've Lost Control" appeared on vinyl in 1986, before 'Acid Tracks' was pressed in 1987 — complicating claims that 'Acid Tracks' was the first acid record.
relationships.evidence: MusicRadar distinguishes the 1986 vinyl appearance of 'I've Lost Control' from the 1987 pressing of 'Acid Tracks.'

relationships.description: Trax Records was founded in 1984 by pressing-plant owner Larry Sherman with Jesse Saunders and Vince Lawrence; Sherman died in April 2020.
relationships.evidence: DJ Mag obituary reports the 1984 founding with Saunders and Lawrence; GO BANG describes Sherman as founder/pressing-plant owner.

relationships.description: Vince Lawrence is credited as a Trax co-founder in some accounts and with label design and initial signings in others; exact founding roles are unsettled.
relationships.evidence: DJ Mag lists Lawrence as co-founder with Sherman; GO BANG credits him with design and signings rather than founding capital.

relationships.description: Jesse Saunders is named as a Trax co-founder in DJ Mag's account; other accounts center Sherman. Role is not fully settled.
relationships.evidence: DJ Mag obituary names Saunders among founders; GO BANG's account emphasizes Sherman with Saunders as co-founder in passing.

relationships.description: Larry Heard (Mr. Fingers) released foundational house works on Trax Records.
relationships.evidence: DJ Mag's Trax history lists Heard among the label's key artists.

relationships.description: Marshall Jefferson released foundational house works on Trax Records.
relationships.evidence: DJ Mag's Trax history lists Jefferson among the label's key artists.

relationships.description: Frankie Knuckles released records on Trax, including the contested 1987 'Your Love.'
relationships.evidence: DJ Mag lists Knuckles among Trax artists; the 'Your Love' credit dispute is separately documented.

relationships.description: Phuture's 'Acid Tracks' was released on Trax Records.
relationships.evidence: DJ Mag's Trax history includes Phuture among the label's releases.

relationships.description: In 2022 Vince Lawrence, Marshall Jefferson, Adonis, Maurice Joshua and others sued Trax alleging unpaid royalties, forged signatures, bounced checks, and poor accounting.
relationships.evidence: DJ Disc Jockey reports the lawsuit and its specific allegations; DJ Mag notes longstanding complaints of missing contracts and poor vinyl quality.

relationships.description: DJ International was founded in 1985 by Rocky Jones and Benji Espinoza.
relationships.evidence: DJ Mag obituary for Espinoza documents the 1985 co-founding.

relationships.description: Benji Espinoza co-founded DJ International with Rocky Jones in 1985 — correcting accounts that credit Jones alone.
relationships.evidence: DJ Mag obituary for Espinoza; Jones's own account of the label's origins.

relationships.description: DJ International began as a record pool linking working DJs and labels before becoming a label.
relationships.evidence: Rocky Jones's quoted account in DJ Mag describes the record-pool origins.

relationships.description: Early DJ International releases included Steve 'Silk' Hurley's 'Music Is the Key' as J.M. Silk.
relationships.evidence: DJ Mag's DJ International history lists the release.

relationships.description: Joe Smooth's 'Promised Land' was released on DJ International Records.
relationships.evidence: DJ Mag's DJ International history lists the release.

relationships.description: DJ International released the landmark 1986 compilation 'The House Sound of Chicago.'
relationships.evidence: DJ Mag's DJ International history documents the 1986 compilation.

relationships.description: Knuckles and Hardy attended each other's sets and engaged in friendly competition, linking the Warehouse and Music Box poles of early house.
relationships.evidence: City of Chicago Warehouse report documents their mutual attendance and friendly rivalry.
relationships.source: City of Chicago, 'The Warehouse' landmark designation report

relationships.description: "On and On" was released on Saunders's own Jes Say Records imprint.
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia documents the Jes Say Records release.

relationships.description: "On and On" was based partly on a bootleg megamix of Mach's 'On & On,' showing early house's recombinant, DJ-driven composition method.
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia documents the Mach megamix as a partial source.

relationships.description: WBMX's Hot Mix 5 broadcasts carried club-born house to a large Black radio audience across Chicago.
relationships.evidence: City landmark report documents WBMX reaching a large audience with Hot Mix 5 live mixes.
relationships.source: City of Chicago, 'The Warehouse' landmark designation report

relationships.description: The block of Jefferson between Jackson and Madison was named Frankie Knuckles Way on August 25, 2004; then–state senator Barack Obama advocated for the honor.
relationships.evidence: City of Chicago Warehouse report documents the 2004 naming and Obama's advocacy.
relationships.source: City of Chicago, 'The Warehouse' landmark designation report

relationships.description: Thomas A. Dorsey served as music director of Pilgrim Baptist Church in Bronzeville from 1932 into the late 1970s, anchoring Chicago gospel institutionally.
relationships.evidence: New Georgia Encyclopedia documents Dorsey's music-director tenure at Pilgrim from 1932 into the late 1970s.

relationships.description: Before his gospel career, Dorsey worked as the blues pianist 'Georgia Tom,' a secular identity he later set aside.
relationships.evidence: New Georgia Encyclopedia records Dorsey's earlier career as blues pianist 'Georgia Tom.'

relationships.description: Dorsey co-founded the National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses in 1933, institutionalizing gospel blues nationally.
relationships.evidence: New Georgia Encyclopedia credits Dorsey with developing, publishing, and promoting gospel blues and co-founding the NCGCC in 1933.
relationships.to: National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses (1933)

relationships.description: Dorsey composed 'Take My Hand, Precious Lord' in 1932, one of the most consequential songs in gospel history.
relationships.evidence: New Georgia Encyclopedia lists 'Precious Lord' among Dorsey's compositions; it became a civil-rights-era standard.

relationships.description: Mahalia Jackson made her professional debut in 1928 at Pilgrim Baptist Church in Bronzeville, for which she was paid $4.
relationships.evidence: WYND/Chicago Tribune retrospective documents the 1928 Pilgrim debut, the $4 fee, and her early work as a maid and laundress.

relationships.description: Thomas Dorsey was Mahalia Jackson's mentor; he described her voice to the Tribune as 'a sort of cry or whine, with a lot of pathos.'
relationships.evidence: WYND quotes Dorsey calling Jackson his mentee and describing her singular voice quality.

relationships.description: During King's August 28, 1963 March on Washington speech, Jackson called out 'Tell them about the dream, Martin!' — after which King departed from his prepared text.
relationships.evidence: WFMT reports Jackson, seated behind King, shouted the line and that adviser Clarence B. Jones affirmed the celebrated passages were delivered extemporaneously; All About Jazz gives the same account.
relationships.to: March on Washington, "I Have a Dream" (1963-08-28)

relationships.description: Jackson was a civil-rights movement figure: she sang at a 1956 Montgomery bus-boycott fundraiser ('I'm not going to charge the pilgrims'), and her Chicago home became an unofficial movement headquarters.
relationships.evidence: mahalia-jackson.com documents the 1956 fundraiser, her close relationship with King, and the Chicago home as movement HQ.

relationships.description: Jackson's longtime home was at 8358 S. Indiana Avenue in Chicago's Chatham neighborhood; it is now a marked historic landmark.
relationships.evidence: Landmark coverage documents the Chatham/Indiana Avenue house and its Chicago Tribune marker.

relationships.description: James Cleveland sang in front of Thomas A. Dorsey at Pilgrim Baptist Church as a boy; Dorsey mentored him and wrote a composition for him.
relationships.evidence: thatericalper.com and EBSCO document Cleveland singing before Dorsey at Pilgrim and Dorsey's mentorship.

relationships.description: Cleveland began as a boy soprano at Pilgrim Baptist, where Dorsey was minister of music and Roberta Martin was choir pianist.
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia's James Cleveland biography documents the Pilgrim choir configuration.

relationships.description: Roberta Martin hired Cleveland as a composer and arranger for her ensemble and published his first composition, 'I Want to See Jesus.'
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia and EBSCO document Martin hiring Cleveland after the Gospelaires and publishing his first composition.

relationships.description: Cleveland organized the Gospel Music Workshop of America in 1968 to teach and spread gospel music; it became the dominant force in modern gospel choral music.
relationships.evidence: EBSCO and the GMWA's own history date the founding to 1968 and describe its national influence.

relationships.description: Cleveland's 1963 live album 'Peace Be Still' sold nearly a million copies to a predominantly Black audience with scant mainstream promotion.
relationships.evidence: thatericalper.com documents the album's ~1M sales and its role in making Cleveland a star.

relationships.description: Cleveland produced and co-wrote songs with Aretha Franklin for her multi-million-selling 'Amazing Grace' album.
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia's Cleveland biography credits him as producer/co-writer on 'Amazing Grace' tracks including 'Precious Memories.'

relationships.description: Both parts of Kanye West's 'Father Stretch My Hands' sample Pastor T. L. Barrett's 'Father I Stretch My Hands'; Barrett is credited as a writer.
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia documents the sample in both Pt. 1 and Pt. 2 and Barrett's writer credit.

relationships.description: Kanye West's 'Touch the Sky' samples Curtis Mayfield's 'Move On Up'; the track was produced by Just Blaze, not West.
relationships.evidence: Discogs release credits identify the 'Move On Up' sample and Just Blaze as producer.

relationships.description: Just Blaze produced 'Touch the Sky' for Kanye West's 'Late Registration.'
relationships.evidence: Discogs release credits list Just Blaze as producer.

relationships.description: Lupe Fiasco's career debut was his feature on 'Touch the Sky.'
relationships.evidence: Discogs and contemporary coverage identify the 'Touch the Sky' verse as Fiasco's debut appearance.

relationships.description: Black Box built 'Ride on Time' on an uncleared sample of Loleatta Holloway's 'Love Sensation'; Holloway sued.
relationships.evidence: NME's history of the record documents the uncleared sample and Holloway's lawsuit.

relationships.description: Model Katrin Quinol mimed Holloway's sampled vocal in public performances of 'Ride on Time,' creating a false public credit.
relationships.evidence: NME documents Quinol miming the vocal while Holloway's sampled voice was the actual recording.

relationships.description: Mahalia Jackson recorded 'Come Sunday' with Duke Ellington, bridging gospel and jazz.
relationships.evidence: All About Jazz documents the Jackson–Ellington 'Come Sunday' recording.

relationships.description: In 1961 Jackson became the first gospel singer to win a Grammy Award, carrying gospel to a larger audience outside the Black church.
relationships.evidence: All About Jazz documents the 1961 Grammy milestone.

relationships.description: On August 4, 1966, Jackson sang 'We Shall Overcome' with MLK, Rev. Jesse Jackson, and Albert Raby at New Friendship Missionary Baptist Church, 844 W. 71st St., Chicago.
relationships.evidence: Chicago Tribune photo archive (via WYND) documents the 1966 Chicago appearance with King.

relationships.description: Leonard Chess co-founded Chess Records in Chicago in 1950 with his brother Phil, building it from Aristocrat Records.
relationships.evidence: Chess Records history documents the 1950 founding by the Chess brothers as successor to Aristocrat (1947).

relationships.description: Phil Chess co-founded Chess Records with Leonard in 1950.
relationships.evidence: Chess Records history documents joint founding by the two brothers.

relationships.description: Chess Records was the successor to Aristocrat Records (founded 1947); the Chess brothers bought out their partners and renamed it in 1950.
relationships.evidence: Chess Records history and GlobeSt.com document the Aristocrat-to-Chess transition in 1950.

relationships.description: Chess Records operated from 2120 S. Michigan Avenue from May 1957 to 1967 — its first owned, self-contained facility; designated a Chicago Landmark on May 16, 1990.
relationships.evidence: City of Chicago Chess landmark report and Chess Records history document the May 1957 move, the 1990 landmark designation, and the Checker/Argo/Cadet subsidiary operations there.
relationships.source: City of Chicago Chess Records Office and Studio landmark report (chicago.gov); Wikipedia "Chess Records"

relationships.description: Chess's first locations were on the South Side, initially at 4750 South Cottage Grove Avenue.
relationships.evidence: Chess Records history lists 4750 S. Cottage Grove as the initial address.

relationships.description: In 1967 Chess relocated to the former Revere Camera building at 320 E. 21st Street, its final Chicago home, before the brothers sold the company shortly before Leonard's 1969 death.
relationships.evidence: Chess Records history documents the 1967 move to 320 E. 21st St. and the sale before Leonard Chess's death.

relationships.description: Ralph Bass was hired as Chess's A&R director to guide the Michigan Avenue operations; the City landmark report dates the hire to 1958, while some histories say 1960.
relationships.evidence: City landmark report says 1958; tsimon.com's Chess history says 1960. Exact year varies by source.
relationships.source: City of Chicago Chess landmark report; tsimon.com

relationships.description: Muddy Waters was Chess's flagship blues artist; his first Chess release was 'Rollin' Stone' in 1950.
relationships.evidence: International Times documents Waters's 1950 'Rollin' Stone' as his first release for the newly renamed Chess label; Far Out notes its influence.

relationships.description: Waters recorded and released 'Rollin' Stone' in 1950, updating the older 'Catfish Blues' tradition; it became one of the most consequential titles in popular music.
relationships.evidence: Far Out and International Times document the 1950 recording and its 'Catfish Blues' lineage.

relationships.description: The Rolling Stones took their band name from Waters's 'Rollin' Stone' — Brian Jones reportedly saw the record lying nearby when asked the band's name in 1962.
relationships.evidence: Far Out, NED Rock, and Parade all document the naming story; International Times notes the adaptation came 12 years after the song's release.

relationships.description: Muddy Waters personally directed Chuck Berry to Leonard Chess, launching Berry's recording career.
relationships.evidence: 56thst.com's Berry history states Berry signed with Chess in 1955 'on Muddy Waters' recommendation.'

relationships.description: Chuck Berry signed with Chess Records in 1955 and became one of its defining rock & roll artists.
relationships.evidence: 56thst.com documents the 1955 signing; Chess histories list Berry among the label's central artists.

relationships.description: Berry recorded 'Maybellene' on May 21, 1955 (adapting 'Ida Red'); released July 1955, it hit #1 R&B and #5 pop and sold over a million copies.
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia's 'Maybellene' entry and 56thst.com document the session date, chart performance, and sales.

relationships.description: DJ Alan Freed received a co-writer credit on 'Maybellene' as payola-by-royalties despite not writing it; Berry told Rolling Stone (1972) Freed 'didn't sit down with me at all and write anything.' The credit was withdrawn in 1986.
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia documents the payola credit mechanism, Berry's 1972 Rolling Stone quote, and the 1986 withdrawal.

relationships.description: Russ Fratto, a printer/stationer to whom Chess owed money, also received a 'Maybellene' co-credit; it was likewise withdrawn in 1986.
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia documents Fratto's credit and its 1986 withdrawal; Bruce Pegg identifies Fratto as the print-shop owner next to Chess's Cottage Grove offices.

relationships.description: Johnnie Johnson played piano on the 'Maybellene' session of May 21, 1955.
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia's 'Maybellene' personnel list credits Johnson on piano.

relationships.description: Willie Dixon played bass on the 'Maybellene' session.
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia's 'Maybellene' personnel list credits Dixon on bass.

relationships.description: Bo Diddley's 1955 debut single 'Bo Diddley' on the Checker subsidiary introduced the beat that became a rock building block.
relationships.evidence: Far Out documents the 1955 Checker release and the beat's long influence.

relationships.description: Howlin' Wolf recorded for Chess after Leonard Chess's field trip to Arkansas; his first record featured James Cotton on harp and Ike Turner on piano.
relationships.evidence: tsimon.com's Chess history documents the signing and first-record personnel.

relationships.description: Little Walter recorded at Chess during its 2120 S. Michigan era.
relationships.evidence: tsimon.com's Chess history lists Little Walter among the artists recording at Chess.

relationships.description: Etta James released records on Chess in the 1960s; sourcing for her exact Chess tenure is thinner than for the core blues roster.
relationships.evidence: tsimon.com lists Etta James among Chess releases; dedicated sourcing not yet located.

relationships.description: Koko Taylor recorded for Chess in the 1960s, including 'Wang Dang Doodle.'
relationships.evidence: tsimon.com lists Koko Taylor among 1960s Chess artists; dedicated sourcing not yet located.

relationships.description: Willie Dixon was Chess's central songwriter, bassist, and producer, writing standards for Waters, Howlin' Wolf, and others.
relationships.evidence: Parade documents Dixon writing 'Hoochie Coochie Man'; Chess histories identify him as songwriter/bassist/producer.

relationships.description: Dixon wrote 'Hoochie Coochie Man,' recorded by Muddy Waters at Chess in January 1954 and released that March; it entered the National Recording Registry in 2004.
relationships.evidence: Parade documents the writing credit, 1954 recording/release, and 2004 Registry induction.

relationships.description: Dixon sued Led Zeppelin in 1985 over 'Whole Lotta Love' (derived from his 'You Need Love,' recorded by Muddy Waters in 1962); the case settled out of court on February 5, 1987, with no trial verdict.
relationships.evidence: Penn State legal-history PDF and ledzepnews.com document the 1985 suit and the February 5, 1987 settlement without a final hearing.

relationships.description: The Rolling Stones recorded at Chess Studios, 2120 S. Michigan Ave., on June 10–11, 1964 (14 tracks in two days), returning November 1964 and May 1965.
relationships.evidence: Discogs sessionography and Graham Reid/Elsewhere document the June 1964 sessions with engineer Ron Malo; Keith Richards's autobiography calls the studio 'hallowed ground.'

relationships.description: The Stones' instrumental '2120 South Michigan Avenue' (Five by Five EP / 12 X 5, 1964) is a tribute to the Chess address where it was recorded.
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia documents the title's reference to the Chess address and the June 1964 recording.

relationships.description: Chess engineer Ron Malo engineered the Stones' June 1964 sessions; Bill Wyman recalled 'Ron Malo got a good sound almost immediately.'
relationships.evidence: Elsewhere/Graham Reid quotes Wyman on Malo's engineering of the four-hour session.

relationships.description: Buddy Guy visited the Stones during their June 1964 Chess sessions; Willie Dixon tried to sell them songs.
relationships.evidence: Elsewhere documents Guy's and Dixon's visits to the session.

relationships.description: Leonard and Phil Chess bought WHFC-1450 AM for $1 million in 1963 and relaunched it April 1, 1963 as WVON — 'The Voice of the Negro.'
relationships.evidence: Congressional Record (multiple tributes) documents the $1M purchase, the April 1, 1963 debut, and the call-letter meaning.

relationships.description: Phil Chess co-owned WVON with Leonard from its 1963 founding.
relationships.evidence: Congressional Record documents both brothers' ownership.

relationships.description: WVON became the voice of Black Chicago — covering the civil rights movement, calming the city after King's assassination, and ranking among the market's top stations.
relationships.evidence: Congressional Record tributes document WVON's civil-rights coverage, the post-MLK-assassination calm appeals, and top-5 ratings.

relationships.description: Pervis Spann, 'The Blues Man,' was hired by the Chess brothers as a WVON DJ in 1963; he staged an 87-hour sleepless 'sit-in' raising money for MLK.
relationships.evidence: Congressional Record (Rush tribute, 2022) documents Spann's hiring and the 87-hour fundraiser.

relationships.description: Herb Kent, 'The Cool Gent,' was one of WVON's heritage 'Good Guys' air personalities.
relationships.evidence: Congressional Record lists Kent among the station's great Black air personalities.

relationships.description: Don Cornelius started in broadcasting at WVON in 1966 after news director Roy Wood — impressed by his voice during a traffic stop — offered him a newsroom job.
relationships.evidence: Black America Web documents the 1966 WVON hiring; Pollstar's Chicago retrospective recounts the Roy Wood traffic-stop story via WVON president Melody Spann Cooper.

relationships.description: Rev. Jesse Jackson called into WVON to report the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.
relationships.evidence: Congressional Record and radio histories document Jackson's call to the station on April 4, 1968.

relationships.description: Motown's Berry Gordy had an arrangement sending every song he produced to WVON before any other station; WVON rotation moved national airplay and sales.
relationships.evidence: Proviso East's WVON history and Wikipedia document Gordy's first-listen arrangement and WVON's national influence.

relationships.description: In 1993 Marie Dixon — widow of Willie Dixon — bought the 2120 S. Michigan building and opened it as a museum in 1997; it now houses Willie Dixon's Blues Heaven Foundation.
relationships.evidence: Chess Records history documents the 1993 purchase and 1997 museum opening.

relationships.description: Vivian Carter founded Vee-Jay Records in 1953 with her husband Jimmy Bracken, building a major Black-owned Chicago label.
relationships.evidence: Signature Sounds' Vee-Jay history documents the 1953 founding by Carter and Bracken.

relationships.description: Jimmy Bracken co-founded Vee-Jay Records with Vivian Carter in 1953.
relationships.evidence: Signature Sounds documents Bracken's co-founding role.

relationships.description: Gene Chandler's 'Duke of Earl' was released on Vee-Jay in late 1961/1962, hitting #1 on both pop and R&B charts and selling a million copies.
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia documents the Vee-Jay release, three weeks at #1, and million-copy sales; Chandler co-wrote it with Bernice Williams and Earl Edwards.

relationships.description: Chandler co-wrote 'Duke of Earl' with Bernice Williams and Earl Edwards; recorded at Universal Recording in Chicago, it became his signature and a Grammy Hall of Fame inductee (2002).
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia documents the songwriting credits, Universal Recording session, and 2002 Grammy Hall of Fame induction.

relationships.description: Curtis Mayfield made his first recordings at age 16 in 1958 as a member of the Impressions, becoming their lead singer, writer, and producer.
relationships.evidence: Divabetic's Mayfield history documents the 1958 start with the Impressions at age 16.

relationships.description: Mayfield founded Curtom Records in March 1968 with manager Eddie Thomas — among the first prominent Black-artist-owned American labels.
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia's Curtom entry and Divabetic document the March 1968 founding by Mayfield and Thomas in Chicago.

relationships.description: Eddie Thomas co-founded Curtom with Mayfield, handling marketing and promotion.
relationships.evidence: Under the Radar's Curtom history documents Thomas as co-founder handling marketing/promotion.

relationships.description: Curtom was a Chicago-based, Black-owned soul label distributed at various times by Buddah, Warner Bros., and RSO.
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia documents Curtom's Chicago location and distributor history.

relationships.description: Mayfield's 'Super Fly' soundtrack (1972) was released on Curtom; its singles 'Freddie's Dead' (#4 pop) and 'Superfly' (#8 pop) made it a landmark that outsold the film.
relationships.evidence: Release histories document the July 11, 1972 Curtom release and the two million-selling singles.

relationships.description: Sam Cooke founded SAR Records in 1961; his son Todd Mayfield's biography says Cooke's artist-ownership model was Curtis Mayfield's direct business template.
relationships.evidence: Reverb, citing Todd Mayfield's 'Traveling Soul,' documents SAR (1961) as Mayfield's model for Curtom and his own publishing company.

relationships.description: Mayfield followed Cooke's path from gospel (Northern Jubilee Gospel Singers) to secular stardom and from artist to owner.
relationships.evidence: Reverb documents Mayfield's gospel-to-secular arc mirroring Cooke's, and his adoption of Cooke's ownership model.

relationships.description: Curtis Mayfield grew up in Chicago's Cabrini-Green housing projects, grounding his socially conscious songwriting in lived experience.
relationships.evidence: Reverb documents Mayfield's Cabrini-Green upbringing.

relationships.description: The Impressions' 'People Get Ready' (1965), written by Mayfield, was embraced by the civil-rights movement and used on freedom rides.
relationships.evidence: Mayfield histories document the 1965 song's adoption by the movement.

relationships.description: Don Cornelius created and hosted 'Soul Train' — the first Black music variety show on American television — launching it on WCIU-TV Chicago in August 1970.
relationships.evidence: Black America Web and Black Enterprise document the August 1970 WCIU launch with Cornelius's own $400 pilot, inspired by American Bandstand but for a Black audience.

relationships.description: 'Soul Train' aired locally on WCIU-TV Chicago from 1970–71, then entered national syndication in October 1971 (premiering October 2, 1971) and ran to 2006.
relationships.evidence: TVIV and Wikipedia document the WCIU run, the October 1971 syndication launch, and the 2006 finale.

relationships.description: Sid McCoy — who had accompanied Cornelius from WVON — was the narrator of 'Soul Train.'
relationships.evidence: Wikipedia's Soul Train credits list McCoy as narrator; Congressional Record notes he accompanied Cornelius from WVON.

relationships.description: Maurice White founded Earth, Wind & Fire in Chicago in 1969, building it from the Salty Peppers; the band later moved to Los Angeles.
